name: Harvest Now Decrypt Later
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The One Quantum Threat That's Real Today
lesson.summary: Adversaries can intercept and store encrypted data now, betting that a future quantum computer capable of running Shor's algorithm will let them decrypt it later, which makes migrating long-lifetime sensitive data to the NIST standards an urgent task rather than a distant one.
lesson.body:
Nearly every chapter in this section has made some version of the same point: quantum computing's threat to encryption is real in theory but not remotely imminent in practice, given the gap between today's hardware and what Shor's algorithm requires. This final chapter covers the one important exception, where the threat is not hypothetical and not years away, because it is already happening right now, regardless of how long a capable quantum computer takes to arrive. It is called "harvest now, decrypt later," and understanding it requires holding together nearly everything covered earlier in this section.

The idea is straightforward. An adversary, whether a government agency, a criminal organization, or a corporate actor, does not need a working quantum computer today to benefit from one in the future. They only need to intercept and store encrypted data now, protected by RSA or elliptic curve cryptography under the assumption, correct as of today, that it cannot be practically decrypted. That data can simply sit archived until a sufficiently capable quantum computer, of the scale discussed in the Massive Qubits Needed chapter, becomes available, at which point Shor's algorithm could be applied retroactively to data intercepted long before that computer existed.

This threat model matters enormously for a specific, narrow category of information: data whose confidentiality needs to last a very long time. Government classified material, certain health records, trade secrets, long term state secrets, and some financial and legal records fall into this category, because their sensitivity does not expire after a year or two, it can remain damaging decades later. For that category, "quantum computers capable of breaking encryption are probably still ten or twenty years away" is not reassuring, because data intercepted today only needs to stay unbroken for as long as its sensitivity lasts, and for state secrets or certain medical records, that can easily exceed a couple of decades.

This is why the previous two chapters matter so much, and why the timing of the NIST standards is not just an abstract accomplishment but a genuinely urgent one. Because post-quantum cryptography already exists in finalized, published form, organizations handling long lifetime sensitive data do not have to wait for a quantum computer to become an active threat before acting. They can migrate to quantum resistant algorithms now, which means data intercepted after that migration stays protected against a future quantum computer, regardless of when, or whether, one is eventually built at the necessary scale. The earlier a system migrates, the smaller the window of data left vulnerable to this attack.

This closes the encryption thread of this section on a note that is neither the breathless alarm of typical media coverage nor a dismissive "quantum computing threatens nothing for decades." Both framings miss the nuanced truth: the mathematical threat is real, current hardware is nowhere close to realizing it, working defenses exist and are now formally standardized, and the one genuinely urgent action is protecting long lifetime sensitive data today, not because a quantum computer is imminent, but because data intercepted today can sit in storage waiting for one indefinitely. That is the calibrated conclusion this guide has been building toward: not "quantum computing is hype, ignore it," and not "quantum computing is an emergency," but a clear eyed reading of what is real, what is exaggerated, what is already solved, and what genuinely deserves attention now.
